validity.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE: confirmed. CAC-2 ('вторая нитка', the second parallel line of the Soviet-era Central Asia-Center (CAC/SAC) transcontinental system) is a real, well-documented pipeline. Gazprom Transgaz Saratov's own corporate history (the sheet's own most-cited existing wiki source, backlinks=7) states explicitly: '1 октября 1970 года — введена в строй вторая нитка газопровода «Средняя Азия — Центр»' (second line commissioned Oct 1 1970) -- this EXACTLY matches GEM's StartYear1=1970. The live corporate site (saratov-tr.gazprom.ru) is unreachable from this environment (connection timeout, not a 404/410), so I verified via a Wayback Machine snapshot instead, which passed url_verifier (HTTP 200 + '1970'/'3600' present). CLASSIFICATION: transmission/Gas is correct -- this is unambiguously a Soviet-built transcontinental trunk gas pipeline, corroborated by multiple sources describing it as 'магистральный газопровод' / trunk line carrying Uzbek/Turkmen gas to Russia. DUPLICATE: checked against the Kazakhstan-gas roster's other two 'Central Asia–Center' rows, P5770 (len 3700, dia 1015/1220/1420) and P5771 (len blank, same diameter set). Per Gazprom Saratov's own history, the CAC system has (at least) FOUR distinct parallel lines: 1st stage/line 1967 (main trunk Kungrad→Voskresensk = 2,062 km, no diameter stated), 2nd line 1970 (no length/diameter stated in the source), 3rd line 1975 (3,600 km, 1220mm), 4th line 1976 (3,700 km, 1220+1420mm). P5770's length (3,700 km) is an EXACT match for the documented 4th line; P5771's diameter set matches P5770 and may be a related/aggregate entry. So P2291/P5770/P5771 most likely represent genuinely distinct PARALLEL PHYSICAL PIPES (not a bibliographic duplicate) -- this is the same legitimate pattern as Bukhara-Ural's two parallel strings. No merge recommended. However, see the separate SPEC finding below: the fact that all three rows carry the IDENTICAL Capacity=60.2 bcm/y is a genuine data-quality caveat, addressed in its own validity entry.

validity.recommendation: Revisit Owner1='Gazprom PJSC' at 100%. Two independent Russian sources say the Kazakh (and Uzbek) SAC segments belong to those countries, with Gazprom's role limited to a transportation/dispatcher contract -- 100% Gazprom ownership of a route GEM itself scopes as Turkmenistan→Russia (crossing Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan) is likely overstated. Consider Owner split by jurisdiction (AO 'Intergas Central Asia' / KazTransGas for the Kazakh section) or at minimum a ResearcherNotes caveat if the row is meant to represent only the Russian-operated portion.
validity.researcher_notes: Two independent, verified sources contradict Owner1=Gazprom PJSC 100%: (1) Samruk-Kazyna (sk.kz) press release 'Информация по сотрудничеству с ОАО «Газпром»' (2011): describes SAC as 'the shortest international transit route for delivering Turkmen and Uzbek gas through Kazakhstan's territory' and states a 2011-2015 CONTRACT (not ownership transfer) governed gas transport through Kazakhstan between Gazprom and AO 'Intergas Central Asia' (ица), with a separate dispatcher agreement for managing/controlling the gas transport systems. (2) Interfax (2009), reporting on a 2009-04-09 pipeline rupture near the Turkmen/Uzbek border: 'Between Russian and Turkmen pipeline sections lie sections of the SAC system belonging to Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan' -- explicit language of national ownership of the transiting segments, with Russia only taking custody of the gas at the Aleksandrov Gai compressor station on the border. Neither source supports Gazprom owning the Kazakh (or Uzbek) legs. If GEM's P2291 row is meant to model the pipe as it physically runs (Turkmenistan→Uzbekistan→Kazakhstan→Russia), a single 100%-Gazprom owner is not well supported by independent sourcing; Gazprom's documented role in Kazakhstan is contractual (transportation/dispatch), not proprietary.

validity.researcher_notes: LENGTH (GEM: 2,662.00 km): no independent source found that supports 2,662 km specifically for the 2nd line. Gazprom Transgaz Saratov's own history (the most authoritative source available, and the one already cited by gem.wiki for this row) gives explicit lengths for three OTHER named segments of the same system, none matching: 1st-stage main trunk Kungrad→Voskresensk = 2,062 km (1967); 3rd line = 3,600 km (1975); 4th line = 3,700 km (1976); the 2nd line's own commissioning entry (1970) states no length at all. 2,062 km is suspiciously close to GEM's 2,662 km (a single-digit '0'↔'6' difference) -- worth flagging as a possible transcription slip, but I cannot confirm this is the actual origin of GEM's number, so I'm not proposing a corrected value, only flagging the gap. CAPACITY (GEM: 60.20 bcm/y): this figure IS independently attested, but only as a WHOLE-SYSTEM / whole-corridor aggregate, never as a single-string figure. A peer-reviewed academic PDF (Neft i Gaz journal, Almaty, March 2019, by two named academics) states: '«Средняя Азия–Центр» в направлении Узбекистан–Казахстан–Россия: ... с пропускной способностью – 60,2 млрд м3/год, протяженностью – 3 962 км (оператор АО «Интергаз Центральная Азия»)' -- i.e. 60.2 bcm/y is stated for the WHOLE Uzbekistan–Kazakhstan–Russia transit corridor at 3,962 km, not for a single 1970-vintage 1220mm line. (Note: url_verifier FAILs the content check on this PDF -- 881KB/16pp, large-PDF extractor miss per the verifier's own documented false-negative class -- but I manually confirmed the exact text via `pdftotext -layout`; HTTP 200 is real and the content is present.) Separately, Interfax (2009) gives yet a THIRD aggregate figure -- 57 bcm/y design capacity, degraded to 52-53 bcm/y actual throughput due to pipe age -- for what it also treats as the whole SAC system. Three different aggregate-capacity figures (57 / 60.2 / and mingas.ru's later 80 bcm/y post-1985 buildout) from three sources, and GEM stamps 60.2 identically onto THREE separate string-level rows (P2291, P5770, P5771). This is the 'one system total on multiple strings' shape flagged by the orchestrator (India/HVJ-style defect) -- 60.2 bcm/y is a real, sourced number, but not evidence that CAC-2 alone carries 60.2 bcm/y of throughput.

Both sources describe SAC as a 'магистральный газопровод' / 'trans-continental trunk pipeline system' -- consistent with 'transmission' classification, not gathering/feeder.

Gazprom Transgaz Saratov's corporate history states exactly: '1 октября 1970 года — введена в строй вторая нитка газопровода «Средняя Азия — Центр»' (Oct 1, 1970: the second line of CAC put into service) -- an exact match for StartYear1=1970 naming this specific line ('CAC-2'). summary: P2291 (CAC-2, the 1970-commissioned second parallel line of the Central Asia-Center system): existence and classification confirmed via Gazprom Transgaz Saratov's own history (exact StartYear1=1970 match) and not a bibliographic duplicate of P5770/P5771 (legitimately separate parallel strings, though see caveat). Two concerns staged: ATTRIBUTION -- Owner1='Gazprom PJSC' 100% is contradicted by two independent sources (Samruk-Kazyna, Interfax) stating the Kazakh/Uzbek SAC segments belong to those countries under a transport contract with Gazprom, not Gazprom ownership. SPEC -- Length 2,662 km matches no documented CAC-2 figure (nearest are 2,062 km for the 1st-stage trunk and 3,600/3,700 km for the 3rd/4th lines), and Capacity 60.2 bcm/y is corroborated only as the whole-system aggregate (also stamped identically on P5770 and P5771), a likely system-total-on-multiple-strings defect. Status/Fuel/PipelineType/StartYear1 filled with verified refs (tier high/medium); Length, Capacity, Diameter, FuelSource, and Location left UNRESOLVED rather than force a weak ref.
